title: University of Bonn Research Associate PhD Positions 2027 in Germany: 12 Fully Funded Doctoral Research Vacancies
summary: The University of Bonn in Germany is inviting applications for 12 Research Associate positions within the DFG Research Training Group 3125, “Reconciliation and its Equivalents in a Transcultural Comparison.” These doctoral research positions offer successful candidates an opportunity to undertake a PhD within an interdisciplinary and international research environment while being employed as research associates at the University of Bonn. The positions are scheduled to commence on February 1, 2027 , and will be offered on fixed-term contracts running until January 31, 2031 . Successful applicants will be employed at 65% and remunerated according to TV-L pay grade 13 (Entgeltgruppe 13) . The Research Training Group brings together researchers from multiple academic disciplines to investigate reconciliation and related approaches to conflict transformation across different societies, cultures and historical periods. The programme combines doctoral research with structured supervision, interdisciplinary academic exchange, professional development and opportunities for international research networking. Applications are particularly relevant to prospective doctoral researchers with academic backgrounds in areas including history, law, social sciences, anthropology, cultural studies, peace and conflict studies, Jewish studies, religious studies, heritage and museum studies, and reconciliation studies. The application deadline is September 17, 2026 . About the University of Bonn Research Associate Positions The DFG Research Training Group 3125, “Reconciliation and its Equivalents in a Transcultural Comparison,” is seeking 12 Research Associates at 65% employment . The positions are designed around doctoral research. Successful candidates will be expected to develop and write a doctoral dissertation addressing a subject that falls within the intellectual and thematic scope of the Research Training Group. The programme offers researchers the opportunity to work within a community dedicated to examining concepts, strategies and practices associated with conflict transformation. Rather than examining reconciliation solely from the perspective of one discipline, historical period or cultural context, the Research Training Group adopts an interdisciplinary and transcultural approach . Its research incorporates both synchronic and diachronic comparative analysis . This means that researchers may examine relevant concepts and practices across different societies and cultures as well as across different historical periods. Research Training Group: “Reconciliation and its Equivalents in a Transcultural Comparison” The central objective of the Research Training Group is to investigate concepts, strategies and practices of conflict transformation through interdisciplinary and transcultural research. Reconciliation can have different meanings depending on historical, cultural, political, religious, legal and social circumstances. Consequently, the programme seeks to investigate reconciliation alongside concepts and practices that may function as its equivalents in different contexts. The Research Training Group therefore provides a framework in which doctoral researchers can contribute subject-specific expertise while participating in broader conversations across academic disciplines. The interdisciplinary nature of the programme creates opportunities for doctoral candidates to consider questions that might otherwise remain confined to individual academic fields. Potential doctoral projects must fall within the scope of the Research Training Group. Applicants should therefore ensure that their proposed research has a clear connection to the programme s focus on reconciliation, equivalent concepts, conflict transformation and transcultural or comparative approaches. The University of Bonn indicates that examples of potential PhD projects and additional information about the Research Training Group can be found through the programme s official website. Number of Available Positions A total of 12 Research Associate positions are available. Each position is offered at 65% employment within the DFG Research Training Group 3125. This recruitment therefore represents an opportunity for a cohort of doctoral researchers from different academic backgrounds to undertake their research within the same interdisciplinary training environment. Position Duration and Starting Date Successful candidates are expected to begin their positions on: February 1, 2027 The contracts will run until: January 31, 2031 The positions are fixed-term appointments in accordance with § 2 (1) WissZeitVG . Applicants should therefore consider their availability to relocate to or work on site at the University of Bonn for the duration of the programme, as active on-site participation is explicitly required. Main Responsibilities of Successful Research Associates Successful applicants will have two major responsibilities within the Research Training Group. 1. Writing a Doctoral Thesis Research associates will be expected to undertake and write a doctoral thesis on a topic falling within the scope of the Research Training Group . The doctoral project will therefore form a central component of the successful applicant s work during the appointment. Applicants are required to submit a five-page project outline as part of their application. This document should enable the selection committee to understand the proposed doctoral research and how it relates to the Research Training Group. 2. Active Participation in Research Training Group Activities Successful candidates must also participate actively and on site in the activities organised by the Research Training Group. This participation will take place as part of the group s study and qualification programme . Applicants should therefore understand that the position is not structured solely around independent dissertation writing. Researchers will become members of an academic community and are expected to participate in its intellectual, training and collaborative activities. Academic Qualifications Required Applicants must possess a university degree completed with above-average results . Accepted qualifications include: A Master s degree; A State Examination; or An equivalent university qualification. The University of Bonn particularly welcomes candidates from disciplines connected with the interdisciplinary work of the Research Training Group. Preferred Academic Fields Applicants preferably have academic backgrounds in one or more of the following subjects: Ancient History; Art History; Critical Museum and Heritage Studies; Early Modern History; English Literature and Cultural Studies; Historical Peace and Conflict Studies; Peace and Conflict Studies; History and Culture of the Islamicate World; History Education; Jewish Studies; Law; Modern and Contemporary History; Philosophy of Religion; Social and Cultural Anthropology; Social Sciences; and Reconciliation Studies. Because the Research Training Group is explicitly interdisciplinary, applicants should carefully explain how their previous academic training and proposed doctoral project relate to the programme s overall research agenda. Interdisciplinary Research Interest In addition to formal academic qualifications, applicants must demonstrate an interest in interdisciplinary work . This requirement is particularly important given the structure of the programme. Researchers from different disciplines will participate in the Research Training Group, meaning successful candidates should be prepared to communicate their research beyond the boundaries of their own academic specialisation. Candidates should be interested in exchanging ideas with researchers working with different methodologies, theoretical traditions, geographic regions and historical periods. English Language Requirements Applicants must possess sufficient English-language proficiency to participate effectively in the programme. The minimum requirement is: English at B2 level However, candidates intending to write their doctoral dissertation in English must have: English at C1 level Proof of English-language proficiency forms part of the application requirements. Importantly, the announcement states that proof of English proficiency may, if necessary, be submitted after the start of employment . Applicants who do not currently possess the required certificate should therefore carefully review the official requirements rather than automatically assuming they are ineligible. Teamwork Requirements Applicants must also demonstrate the ability to work effectively in a team . The Research Training Group is designed around interdisciplinary collaboration and academic exchange. Candidates should therefore be comfortable working within a research community rather than pursuing their doctoral research entirely independently. The ability to communicate ideas, receive feedback, contribute to discussions and cooperate with colleagues from different academic backgrounds will be important. Benefits of the University of Bonn Research Associate PhD Positions Successful candidates will receive access to a substantial range of academic, professional and institutional opportunities during their doctoral studies. Subject-Specific Doctoral Research The programme offers excellent opportunities to undertake a subject-specific doctoral thesis while simultaneously participating in a broader interdisciplinary environment. Researchers can therefore maintain the disciplinary depth required for doctoral research while gaining exposure to perspectives from other fields. International and Interdisciplinary Environment Successful applicants will become part of an interdisciplinary and international research environment . This may be particularly valuable for researchers whose projects involve comparative, transcultural or international dimensions. Intensive Academic Exchange The programme provides opportunities for intensive academic and interdisciplinary exchange . Researchers will have opportunities to engage with scholars working on related questions from different disciplinary and methodological perspectives. International Academic Networking The Research Training Group also provides opportunities for international academic networking . This includes the possibility of receiving funding for a research stay abroad lasting several months . Such research stays may enable doctoral researchers to undertake archival work, field research, institutional visits, academic collaborations or other activities relevant to their dissertations, depending on their individual projects. Structured Doctoral Supervision Successful candidates will benefit from a structured supervision framework for doctoral studies . Structured supervision can be particularly valuable during a PhD because it provides researchers with an organised framework for receiving academic guidance and progressing through different stages of their doctoral projects. Study and Qualification Programme Researchers will have access to a comprehensive study and qualification programme . Importantly, participants will also have opportunities to help shape the programme themselves . This creates scope for doctoral researchers to contribute to the academic and professional development environment in which they participate. Collegial and Family-Friendly Working Environment The University of Bonn states that successful researchers will work within a collegial and family-friendly environment . This is intended to support researchers as they undertake the demanding combination of doctoral research, academic development and participation in the activities of the Research Training Group. Salary and Employment Conditions The positions are remunerated according to: TV-L Pay Grade 13 / Entgeltgruppe 13 Each Research Associate position is offered at 65% . Applicants should note that the vacancy announcement identifies the applicable German public-sector pay classification rather than stating a single fixed salary amount. Actual remuneration may therefore depend on the applicable employment and salary rules. Required Application Documents Candidates interested in applying should prepare a complete application . The required materials include: References Curriculum Vitae (CV) Two-page cover letter Five-page project outline Proof of English-language proficiency Letters of recommendation Applicants should pay careful attention to the special instructions concerning the English-language certificate and recommendation letters. Proof of English Proficiency Proof of English-language proficiency is requested as part of the application documentation. However, according to the vacancy announcement, it may be submitted after the start of employment if necessary . Letters of Recommendation Letters of recommendation may be submitted if the candidate is invited to an interview . Applicants should nevertheless identify potential referees early enough to ensure that recommendation letters can be provided if requested during the selection process. Five-Page PhD Project Outline One of the most significant elements of the application is the required five-page project outline . Because successful candidates will spend the appointment working toward a doctoral thesis, the project proposal is likely to play an important role in demonstrating the candidate s academic preparation and the relevance of their proposed research to the Research Training Group. Applicants should ensure that their proposed project falls within the scope of “Reconciliation and its Equivalents in a Transcultural Comparison.” The University of Bonn has indicated that information about the Research Training Group, the group of applicants and examples of potential PhD projects are available through the programme s website. Candidates should consult these resources when developing their proposals so they can understand the broader intellectual environment in which their doctoral research would be situated. How to Apply Applications must be submitted by email . Candidates should send their complete applications to: ckrueger@uni-bonn.de The application must include the following application code: 2026/333 Applicants should ensure that the application code is correctly included so that their submission can be associated with the appropriate recruitment process. There is also an important technical requirement concerning the format of applications. Applications may only be submitted by email as a single PDF file. Candidates should therefore combine all application documents that are required at the initial application stage into one PDF rather than sending several separate attachments. Before submitting, applicants should check that: All required documents are included; The documents appear in a logical order; The PDF opens correctly; All pages are readable; The CV is current; The cover letter does not exceed the requested two pages; The project outline follows the requested five-page length; The application code 2026/333 is included; and The application is sent before the deadline. APPLY NOW Application Deadline The deadline for submitting applications is: September 17, 2026 Candidates should aim to submit their applications ahead of the deadline whenever possible. Because applications can only be submitted electronically as a single PDF, applicants should allow enough time to combine and review their documents before sending them. Late applications should not be assumed to receive consideration unless the University of Bonn explicitly states otherwise. Calls for Application PDF file Selection Interviews The University of Bonn states that selection interviews will take place during the first half of October 2026 . Applicants who progress beyond the initial application stage should therefore be prepared for an interview during this period. Candidates invited to interview may also be required to submit their letters of recommendation, as indicated in the vacancy announcement. Important Dates at a Glance Prospective applicants should keep the following timeline in mind: Vacancy announcement published: July 21, 2026 Application deadline: September 17, 2026 Selection interviews: First half of October 2026 Employment and doctoral research start date: February 1, 2027 Contract end date: January 31, 2031 Contact for Further Information Candidates who need additional information about the positions may contact Prof. Dr. Christine Krüger or another member of the team of principal investigators. The programme also provides the following general contact information: Email: reconciliation@uni-bonn.de Telephone: +49 228 73690-36 Applicants can obtain additional information about the Research Training Group through its official website at www.reconciliation.de . Prospective applicants are encouraged to review the official Research Training Group information and available examples of potential PhD projects before preparing their applications. Who Should Consider Applying? These positions may be particularly attractive to early-career researchers who have completed a Master s degree, State Examination or equivalent qualification with strong academic results and now wish to pursue doctoral research. They may also appeal to researchers interested in studying reconciliation and conflict transformation from historical, social, cultural, political, legal, philosophical, religious or anthropological perspectives. Because the programme emphasises interdisciplinary and transcultural comparison, candidates should be willing to engage with perspectives beyond their primary discipline. Applicants should also be comfortable participating actively in an academic community and attending Research Training Group activities on site. Why This Doctoral Research Opportunity Is Significant The University of Bonn s recruitment of 12 Research Associates creates an opportunity for doctoral researchers to undertake individual research projects while participating in a structured cohort. Doctoral research can often involve highly specialised individual work. The Research Training Group supplements that process with structured supervision, interdisciplinary exchange, qualification activities and international networking. Another notable feature is the potential support for research stays abroad lasting several months . The combination of doctoral research, salaried employment, structured supervision and academic development makes these positions particularly relevant for candidates seeking to pursue a PhD within an organised research environment. Application Checklist Before sending an application, candidates should confirm that they have addressed the following requirements: Hold a Master s degree, State Examination or equivalent university qualification; Have completed the qualification with above-average results; Have a proposed doctoral project relevant to the Research Training Group; Have an interest in interdisciplinary research; Meet the English-language requirement of at least B2; Have C1 English if planning to write the dissertation in English; Be able to work effectively within a team; Be prepared for active on-site participation; Prepare references; Prepare an updated CV; Write a two-page cover letter; Prepare a five-page doctoral project outline; Arrange proof of English-language proficiency, subject to the stated possibility of later submission; Be prepared to provide recommendation letters if invited to interview; Combine the required initial application materials into a single PDF; Include application code 2026/333 ; Submit the application by email to ckrueger@uni-bonn.de ; and Submit the application no later than September 17, 2026 . Conclusion The University of Bonn Research Associate PhD positions for 2027 provide an opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers to pursue advanced research on reconciliation, conflict transformation and related concepts within the DFG Research Training Group 3125, “Reconciliation and its Equivalents in a Transcultural Comparison.” With 12 Research Associate positions available, the programme brings together researchers from a wide range of academic disciplines and provides a structured setting for doctoral research, interdisciplinary collaboration and international academic engagement. title: Yale Global Health Emerging Scholars Program 2027–2028: Applications Open for NIH-Supported Research Training in 15 Countries
summary: Applications are now open for the Global Health Emerging Scholars Program 2027–2028 , an intensive, 12-month global health research training opportunity supported by the United States National Institutes of Health. The program brings together emerging researchers, health professionals, experienced faculty members and established research institutions in the United States and selected low- and middle-income countries. Participants undertake full-time, mentored research intended to address major population-health challenges while developing the scientific, analytical and leadership capabilities required for long-term careers in global health. The Global Health Emerging Scholars program is administered through a consortium comprising Yale University, Stanford University, the University of Arizona and the University of California, Berkeley . Its international research network currently covers 15 countries across Africa, South America, Asia, the Middle East and Oceania. Applications for the 2027–2028 program must be submitted by October 1, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. United States Eastern Time . The official Stanford consortium page confirms that the upcoming program year is expected to run from July 2027 to June 2028. Applicants should account for time-zone differences and avoid waiting until the closing hours to submit their materials. See the official 2027–2028 announcement . Key Program Details Program name: Global Health Emerging Scholars Program Participating U.S. universities: Yale University, Stanford University, University of Arizona and University of California, Berkeley Program year: 2027–2028 Duration: 12 months Expected period: July 2027 to June 2028 Commitment: Full-time, normally approximately 40 hours per week Training model: Mentored research, professional development and structured learning Research locations: Participating institutions in 15 low- and middle-income countries Application deadline: October 1, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time Application method: Online through the Yale application portal Program support: Monthly stipend, research support and specified travel and training expenses Official program page: Yale Global Health Emerging Scholars Program Online application: Complete the GHES application What Is the Global Health Emerging Scholars Program? The Global Health Emerging Scholars Program provides intensive research training for individuals seeking to become productive, independent researchers and leaders in global health. It is part of the Launching Future Leaders in Global Health Research Training Program , commonly known as LAUNCH. This wider initiative is sponsored by the Fogarty International Center and collaborating institutes and centers within the U.S. National Institutes of Health. Rather than offering only classroom-based instruction, the program places participants within established medical and research institutions where they complete a defined research project under the supervision of experienced U.S. and LMIC faculty mentors. The participating institutions have long-standing relationships developed through collaborative research, joint funding, academic partnerships and mentorship. These institutions also maintain research oversight, ethical-review systems and active research portfolios, creating an environment in which participants can receive practical guidance throughout the research process. Mission and Purpose of the Program The central mission of the program is to develop new communities of researchers, educators and professionals capable of responding to emerging global health challenges. The program has historically paid particular attention to health problems associated with rapid urbanization, poverty, social inequalities and the expansion of informal settlements. These environments frequently face multiple interconnected challenges, including inadequate healthcare access, overcrowding, environmental hazards, infectious diseases, noncommunicable diseases and limited public resources. Instead of addressing each disease or health condition in isolation, the program encourages a comprehensive and multidisciplinary approach. Participants are expected to examine the social, environmental, economic, clinical and institutional factors that influence population health. The program particularly encourages research that: Improves access to affordable and high-quality healthcare in resource-limited settings; Develops practical interventions for communities facing social and economic inequalities; Strengthens the management of scarce health resources; Improves the effectiveness of healthcare systems and services; Produces scalable solutions that can be implemented in real-world settings; Responds to health challenges created by rapid urbanization; Strengthens local research and institutional capacity; and Translates scientific evidence into measurable health improvements. Supported Research Areas Applicants may propose research across a broad range of global health disciplines. Areas identified by the program include, but are not limited to: Chronic and noncommunicable diseases; HIV, sexually transmitted infections and other infectious diseases; Environmental health; Maternal and child health; Health-system delivery and access; Mental health; Intentional and unintentional injuries; Trauma and emergency care; Urban health; Poverty and health inequalities; Resource management in healthcare; Implementation science; Population health interventions; and Innovative approaches to improving health services. Applicants should select a research area that corresponds with the expertise and active research portfolio of their proposed training site. A strong application requires more than a broadly relevant idea: the project must also be feasible to implement and complete within the 12-month program period. Structured Training Curriculum The program combines mentored research with a structured curriculum intended to strengthen both technical and professional capabilities. Innovation Design Participants learn how to design practical and scalable solutions for real-world global health problems. This component emphasizes interventions that can function within the financial, institutional and operational limitations of resource-constrained settings. Rigor and Reproducibility This component focuses on high-quality research design, data integrity, ethical research practices and the production of findings that can be verified and reproduced. Fellows are expected to develop a strong understanding of reliable scientific methodology. Leadership Leadership training develops participants’ abilities in communication, collaboration, multidisciplinary teamwork and team science. These skills are especially important for global health researchers who must frequently work across institutions, cultures, professions and national boundaries. Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Participants are introduced to analytical tools and methods that support data-driven global health research. The inclusion of data science and artificial intelligence reflects the increasing importance of advanced analytics in public-health surveillance, research design, program evaluation and health decision-making. Mentorship Development The program also operates a Mentoring-the-Mentor initiative for alumni. This strengthens the program’s long-term mentorship network and enables former participants to support the professional development of future researchers. Participating Research Countries The current Yale research-site directory and eligibility page enumerate 15 participating countries. Africa Burkina Faso Ethiopia Kenya Nigeria Senegal Tanzania Uganda South America Colombia Ecuador Peru South and Southeast Asia Bangladesh India Malaysia Middle East Lebanon Oceania Samoa Applicants should not select a country solely because of geographical preference. They must identify a site where the available mentors, institutional resources and active research programs align with their proposed subject. Main Applicant Streams The program has three principal applicant streams: U.S. postdoctoral applicants, U.S. predoctoral applicants and eligible LMIC postdoctoral applicants. U.S. Postdoctoral Applicants U.S. postdoctoral applicants must: Be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident; Hold a doctoral or qualifying health-professional degree by the beginning of the training period; Normally be within five years of completing their terminal doctoral degree; If applying with a health-professional degree, normally be within five years of completing clinical training; Have a professional relationship with an eligible GHES faculty mentor; Obtain the support of both a designated U.S. mentor and a designated LMIC mentor; and Be able to spend approximately 10 to 12 months at the selected LMIC research site. Recognized qualifications include PhD, DrPH, MD, DO, DVM, DDS and other comparable doctoral or health-professional degrees. A recently completed master’s degree does not restart the five-year eligibility period. If an applicant obtained the relevant terminal degree more than five years ago, completing a master’s degree within the last five years does not ordinarily make that person eligible. U.S. Predoctoral Applicants U.S. predoctoral applicants must: Be a U.S. citizen or permanent resident; Be enrolled in a doctoral or qualifying health-professional degree program; Have passed the relevant qualifying examinations by the application date; Secure the required U.S. and LMIC mentor support; Be prepared to interrupt their formal studies when necessary to undertake full-time research; and Be able to spend approximately 10 to 12 months at the selected LMIC site. Students in programs leading to qualifications such as a PhD, DrPH, MD, DO, DDS, DVM or another eligible doctoral or professional degree may be considered. A predoctoral applicant who will complete the qualifying degree by July 1 of the program year may apply through the postdoctoral stream. If selected, the applicant must provide proof of degree completion before formally starting the program. LMIC Postdoctoral Applicants Applicants using the LMIC postdoctoral route must: Be citizens of one of the currently listed collaborating countries; Reside at or be connected to a participating research location; Hold a doctoral or qualifying health-professional degree at the time of application; Normally be within five years of completing the terminal degree or relevant clinical training; Be affiliated with a participating GHES medical or research institution, or have the required professional relationship with GHES-affiliated faculty; Obtain the endorsement of the designated U.S. and LMIC mentors; and Be able to devote the complete 12-month period to the program. Eligible qualifications may include PhD, DrPH, MBBS, MBChB, MD, MMed, DVM, DDS and other comparable professional or doctoral qualifications. LMIC applicants are not currently accepted for predoctoral placements. Master’s and undergraduate students are also not eligible. Applicants should review the complete official GHES eligibility requirements before contacting mentors or developing a proposal. Important Clarification for Applicants Outside the Four U.S. Universities Yale’s current eligibility information states that U.S. citizens and permanent residents from any U.S. college or university may apply if they establish the required professional relationship with a GHES faculty mentor. However, current consortium guidance also advises applicants outside Yale, Stanford, the University of Arizona and UC Berkeley to contact a program manager for approval or confirmation. Certain U.S. doctoral students may need to establish an affiliation, such as visiting-student status, with one of the consortium institutions. Applicants outside the four participating universities should therefore obtain confirmation from the relevant program manager before investing substantial time in the application. Applicants Who Are Not Eligible According to the official program frequently asked questions , the following individuals are not currently eligible: Undergraduate students; Students enrolled only in a master’s program; LMIC-based doctoral students applying for a predoctoral position; International students in the United States who cannot provide proof of U.S. citizenship or permanent residence; LMIC applicants who cannot secure an affiliation or appointment with a participating research site; U.S. applicants who cannot spend the required period at an LMIC research site; Applicants who cannot commit themselves full-time for the complete program period; and Unaffiliated postdoctoral applicants who cannot secure an appropriate appointment or institutional arrangement through a GHES mentor. Mandatory Mentorship Requirement This is a mentored research training program. Applicants cannot independently submit a research idea and arrange mentorship after selection. Every applicant must have: A primary GHES U.S. mentor from Yale University, Stanford University, the University of Arizona or UC Berkeley; and A primary GHES LMIC mentor affiliated with a participating research institution. Additional mentors may be proposed, but the two designated primary mentors remain compulsory. Applicants who already work with non-GHES mentors must obtain endorsement from the designated GHES mentors. The existing mentors must also be prepared to collaborate with the official mentor team. Applicants should select mentors whose expertise, publications and ongoing research align with the proposed project. The mentors are expected to contribute to the proposal, training plan, research timeline and overall application. Program Commitments Selected participants must comply with demanding time and mobility requirements. Full-Time Participation The program requires a full-time commitment for 12 months. Full-time participation normally means approximately 40 hours of work per week and 100% professional effort devoted to the program. Participants cannot maintain another full-time, temporary or part-time job during the program period. LMIC Placement for U.S. Participants U.S. participants must spend approximately 10 to 12 months at their selected LMIC research training site. Applicants who cannot relocate for this period should not apply. U.S. Training Experience for LMIC Participants LMIC participants undertake most of their work at their affiliated home-country site. They must also participate in a one- to three-month training experience at the university of their primary U.S. mentor. This U.S. component should be designed around the participant’s specific learning needs and may include structured instruction, skills development, professional networking and mentoring. NIH Orientation All selected participants must attend a compulsory five-day orientation at the National Institutes of Health in Bethesda, Maryland. The orientation is anticipated to take place in mid-July at the beginning of the program year. Ongoing Mentor Supervision Participants must work closely with both primary mentors throughout the year. Significant changes to the project or training plan must be discussed with and approved by both mentors before implementation. Financial and Program Support The official program information states that selected participants receive: A monthly stipend for 12 months; Funding for research-related expenses, including relevant laboratory supplies and reagents; International health insurance for U.S. participants; Required vaccinations for U.S. participants; Eligible visa and passport fees; Round-trip international travel to the training site for U.S. participants; and Travel and accommodation associated with the compulsory NIH orientation. The precise stipend amount is not published on the current program page. Applicants should request the applicable rate from the relevant program manager. Stipends may be taxable under U.S. or international tax laws. Participants should seek appropriate tax guidance based on their citizenship, residence and research location. The program does not cover tuition or academic fees for an applicant’s doctoral degree. Applicants who already receive another form of support may be considered for partial assistance. For example, the program may provide research and travel funding where an existing institutional award already covers the applicant’s stipend. How to Apply Applicants should begin preparing well in advance. Yale advises competitive candidates to allow at least six weeks for the process because identifying mentors and developing a realistic research proposal require substantial coordination. Step 1: Confirm Your Eligibility Carefully review the citizenship, degree, training-completion, institutional-affiliation and mobility requirements. Step 2: Select a Research Area Choose a research question relevant to the program’s mission and appropriate for completion within 12 months. Step 3: Identify a Research Training Site Review the participating countries, institutions, available mentors and research specialties. Select a site whose active research corresponds with your proposed project. Step 4: Contact Potential Mentors Approach suitable U.S. and LMIC mentors professionally. Applicants should be prepared to provide: A current curriculum vitae; An NIH biosketch; A short research-project abstract; A description of their research interests; The proposed research location; and An explanation of how their background aligns with the mentor’s work. Step 5: Contact the Appropriate Program Manager Once a U.S. mentor has been identified, notify the program manager at that mentor’s university. Program managers can explain requirements, assess possible eligibility issues and help connect applicants with faculty mentors. Step 6: Develop the Research and Training Plans Applicants should develop their proposal with substantial input from both mentors. The proposal should be scientifically sound, locally relevant, ethically appropriate and achievable within one year. Step 7: Prepare the Supporting Documents All required supporting documents should be completed, checked and converted into the requested formats before submission. Step 8: Submit the Online Application Submit the complete application through the official Yale online application portal no later than October 1, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The portal can save a partially completed application using the applicant’s computer IP address. Applicants should avoid creating or submitting multiple applications. Application Sections and Required Documents The online application contains sections covering: Eligibility; Personal and contact information; Institutional affiliation and citizenship; Professional and academic background; Foreign-language capabilities; Research experience; Publications and conference abstracts; Career goals; Selected research site; U.S. and LMIC mentors; Mentorship plan; Training plan; Institutional Review Board approvals; Project timeline; Research proposal; and Supplemental documentation. Predoctoral candidates must also provide an unofficial academic transcript. Research Proposal Applicants must follow the official proposal instructions exactly. Yale warns that proposals containing missing information or incorrect formatting will not be reviewed. Letters of Recommendation and Support Applicants must submit at least two and no more than three letters. The required letters include: One letter from the primary U.S. mentor at Yale, Stanford, the University of Arizona or UC Berkeley; and One letter from the primary LMIC mentor at the proposed research site. Each letter should: Appear on institutional letterhead; State the mentor’s name, position and institution; Include the mentor’s email address, telephone number and work address; Be addressed to the Global Health Emerging Scholars Fellowship Selection Committee; Be signed by the mentor; and Be uploaded as a scanned or saved PDF file. Applicant NIH Biosketch Applicants must upload an NIH Biographical Sketch Common Form completed and certified through SciENcv. Since January 25, 2026, NIH no longer uses a separate fellowship-specific biosketch format. An ORCID identifier linked to the applicant’s eRA Commons profile is now required. Mentor NIH Biosketches Applicants must also upload Common Form NIH biosketches for their primary U.S. and LMIC mentors. These should likewise be completed and certified through SciENcv. Applicants preparing an NIH biosketch for the first time are strongly encouraged to ask a mentor to review it before submission. Full requirements are available on the official application-process page . Selection Process Applications are initially reviewed and scored by an external panel. Reviewers assess five main areas: The candidate’s potential to succeed as a GHES participant; Aptitude for and interest in research; Potential to build a career in global health; The quality and feasibility of the research proposal; and The strength of the mentoring and training plan. The program’s principal investigators may conduct online interviews when additional assessment is necessary. Final decisions are made by the GHES Executive Committee based on the complete application, research proposal, supporting documents, external reviews and numerical scores. The first round of offers is expected to be issued in April 2027. A second round may be issued between May and June 2027. What Makes a Competitive Application? A strong applicant should begin preparing at least six weeks before the deadline and demonstrate: A consistent academic or professional interest in global health research; Relevant research, clinical, public-health or implementation experience; A clear commitment to a long-term career in global health; A focused and feasible research question; Strong alignment between the proposal and the selected research site; Evidence of meaningful engagement with both primary mentors; A realistic 12-month research and training plan; Awareness of the local context in which the research will take place; Appropriate consideration of ethics and regulatory approvals; Relevant publications, abstracts, technical work or research outputs where available; Suitable language skills or a credible plan for working in the selected setting; and A clear explanation of how the program will contribute to the applicant’s scientific independence and professional development. Applicants should avoid submitting a generic proposal without prior mentor involvement. Mentor suitability, research experience, publication record and commitment to the applicant are directly considered during evaluation. Program Impact The program has operated since 2012 and has developed an international network of researchers, institutions and mentors. As of summer 2026, Yale reports: 224 program alumni; 21 current participants; More than 707 peer-reviewed publications associated with alumni; An average of approximately three peer-reviewed publications per participant after completion; 75% of alumni working primarily in research; 10% working primarily in teaching; and 15% working primarily in clinical practice. The program reports that alumni continue to work in global health research, education or practice. Many have secured competitive grants, progressed toward independent-investigator positions and assumed leadership roles in universities, government institutions and international health organizations. Former participants also return as mentors, contributing to a continuing cycle of research-capacity development.
